report.source_text: Because of the existence of these cerebral complications, we carried out tests for acquired and inherited thrombophilia. Anticardiolipin and antiphospholipid antibodies were assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. The plasma homocysteine level was measured also by an automated immunoassay method. Analyses of protein S (PS), protein C (PC), antithrombin (AT), and activated protein C resistance (APCr) were carried out. The patient was then immediately treated with heparin at 25×103 IU. Results from the workup for hypercoagulability for homocysteine, and antiphospholipid and anticardiolipin antibodies were unremarkable except D-dimers of 1227 ng/mL (normal, <500). APCr activity was negative. Her PC, PS, and AT levels were 97%, 84%, and 82%, respectively (normal, 80%-120%).

clinician.final_diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVT) in a patient with homozygous Factor V Leiden (FVL) mutation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 15-year-old girl from a consanguineous Tunisian family presented with a 4-month history of progressive holocranial headache that became nocturnal and continuous for 45 days, accompanied by visual blurring. On admission, she was alert with normal vitals but exhibited bilateral papilledema and reduced visual acuity (unable to count fingers). Brain CT was unremarkable, but MRI with gadolinium revealed a linear filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus, confirming cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Genetic testing identified homozygous FVL mutation; other thrombophilia markers (prothrombin G20210A, MTHFR C677T, anticardiolipin antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, homocysteine) were negative or normal. Protein C, protein S, and antithrombin levels were within normal limits. Elevated D-dimers (1227 ng/mL) and elevated platelet count (544,000/mm³) supported the thrombotic state. The patient was treated with intravenous heparin followed by a 6-month course of coumarin, resulting in complete resolution of CVT. At 3-year follow-up, she was asymptomatic with unremarkable neurological examination and intact visual acuity.
